explanation: Fires on the token that begins the next item in a repetitive structured sequence, mostly in code/markup/data, where the same kind of element appeared just before. Examples are a second 'btn' class, another 'import'/'#include' line, the next JSON key quote, the next '@' doc tag, the next '$' price in a list, or a repeated 'Why'. Strongest in code/markup; ordinary prose gives only weak activation.

Fires on a token that continues or completes a multi-token named entity or formal title. Examples are surname pieces (Galper-in, Co-oley), parts of organization or institution names (Biolog-ics, Bow-ery, Institut für), degree or certification fields ('degree in communications', 'creative writing'), and URL/handle segments. Generic words outside such names give little or no activation.

Fires on a noun (or its possessive 's) naming a non-human entity that is treated as an agent with its own behavior or will. Examples are 'the body', 'the immune system', 'nature', 'God/the Lord', 'evolution', and software or systems like Windows, TypeScript, 'the runtime' or 'the optimizer', usually as the subject of an action or as the one being asked to do something. Ordinary nouns used non-agentively stay weak.

Fires inside LaTeX math on tokens that join an operator or delimiter to the start of a new group or command. Examples are '(\', '{\', '=\', '^{-', '^{', '_{', '}{' and '-\' (e.g. \frac{\..., e^{\pi(\frac, \sum_{n=1}). Text outside LaTeX is near zero.

Fires on a token that repeats the token(s) immediately before it in a run of repetition. Examples are '♪♪', repeated zero-width or BOM characters, '... ...', 'bla-bla', 'haha'/'hehe', repeated emoji, 'no, no, no', 'old, old, old', repeated digits in long numbers and runs of whitespace. Longer runs of identical tokens give stronger activation.

Fires on 'school' (also 'grade', 'college', 'High School') used as an education-level word, especially as a modifier for pupils: 'schoolchildren', 'high school students', 'sixth grade teachers', 'middle school'. It is strongest when the phrase describes children or students in a demographic or research context.

Extremely sparse: fires only on a '0' digit inside a long run of zeros in a timestamp's fractional-seconds field (e.g. '15:49:15.000000000 +0'). Everything else is essentially zero (about 2% or less).

Fires mostly in non-English text (Portuguese, Spanish, German, French, Danish), on function words (que, se, você, onde, für) and on mid-word subword pieces. A weaker second job is mid-word fragments of rare or unusual words and names in English, such as all-caps legal text, gene names and misspellings. Ordinary English words are weak.

Fires on tokens that open a markup element. In indented HTML/XML that is the '<' after leading whitespace (<meta, <script, <option, <item) and the '"></' closing a script/tag. In LaTeX it is the '\' starting a command (\ldots, \cdot, \begin, \item). Also mildly on 'java' after 'import'.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a word that the tokenizer splits into pieces, very often a 'ch'/'Ch'/'CH' or Cyrillic 'ч' piece, or a short consonant-onset piece like 'p' or 'fr'. This mostly happens in non-English or rare words and names (чистом, pobreza, chuffed, chimp, Gurdaspur, Pujol). Whole common words are weak.

Fires in news, sports and political narrative prose on the predicate or relational word that follows a subject. The clearest cluster is naming/labeling verbs (call, termed, labeled, calling, blacklist). Other activating words include 'know' in 'didn't know'/'I know them', 'of' in phrases like 'one of'/'end of'/'video of', and action verbs (sacked, optioned). These do not form one clean concept.
